title: Week 6 · Lesson 16: Hematology — FNP-Level Approach
html:
PHASE 1 · ADVANCED PATHOPHYSIOLOGY + CLINICAL REASONING

Week 6 — Lesson 16: Hematology

FNP-level goal

Use red-cell physiology, platelet/coagulation mechanisms, and thrombosis risk to approach anemia, bleeding, and venous thromboembolism safely. Build a mechanism-based differential and identify when low hemoglobin, active bleeding, DVT, or PE requires emergency escalation.

Learning Objectives

  • Explain anemia as a mismatch between oxygen-carrying capacity and physiologic demand.
  • Use MCV, reticulocyte response, and clinical context to build a first anemia differential.
  • Differentiate platelet/primary hemostasis problems from coagulation/secondary hemostasis problems.
  • Apply Virchow’s triad to DVT and PE risk.
  • Recognize bleeding, severe anemia, DVT, and PE red flags that are unsafe for routine outpatient follow-up.

Part 1 — Red cells and tissue oxygen delivery

Hemoglobin carries most oxygen in blood. Tissue oxygen delivery depends on oxygen content and perfusion, so anemia can worsen dyspnea, fatigue, dizziness, angina, or exercise intolerance—particularly in patients with CAD, heart failure, lung disease, or limited physiologic reserve. A normal pulse oximetry reading does not rule out clinically important anemia because saturation describes the percentage of hemoglobin bound to oxygen, not how much hemoglobin is present.

Think mechanistically: oxygen delivery ≈ cardiac output × arterial oxygen content. Low hemoglobin lowers oxygen content; the body may compensate with tachycardia and increased cardiac output, but compensation can fail in severe or rapidly developing anemia.

Part 2 — The first anemia framework

Start with three questions: Is blood being lost? Is red-cell production inadequate? Are red cells being destroyed? Then use the mean corpuscular volume (MCV) and reticulocyte response to organize the differential.

Microcytic anemia suggests impaired hemoglobin synthesis; iron deficiency is common, but thalassemia and anemia of inflammation may also be relevant. Normocytic anemia can reflect acute blood loss, chronic disease/inflammation, kidney disease with reduced erythropoietin, hemolysis, or early nutritional deficiency. Macrocytic anemia raises consideration of vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol/liver disease, medications, hypothyroidism, reticulocytosis, and marrow disorders.

Part 3 — Reticulocytes: is the marrow responding?

Reticulocytes are immature red cells. A high reticulocyte response suggests the marrow is reacting appropriately to peripheral loss or destruction, such as acute bleeding or hemolysis. An inappropriately low response suggests reduced production, as in nutrient deficiency, kidney disease, marrow suppression, or chronic inflammation. Interpret the count with the severity of anemia rather than as an isolated number.

Part 4 — Iron deficiency is a diagnosis with a cause

Iron deficiency reduces hemoglobin synthesis and often produces microcytosis as it progresses. The FNP task is not to stop at “low iron.” Ask why: menstrual loss, GI blood loss, pregnancy, reduced intake/absorption, malabsorption, or another cause. In adults—especially men and postmenopausal women—unexplained iron-deficiency anemia should prompt evaluation for occult blood loss and appropriate referral/workup rather than indefinite empiric replacement alone.

Part 5 — B12 deficiency: blood and nervous system

Vitamin B12 deficiency can cause macrocytic anemia and neurologic manifestations such as paresthesias, gait difficulty, cognitive changes, or loss of proprioception. Folate deficiency can also produce macrocytosis but does not produce the same neurologic pattern. Treating a presumed folate deficiency without recognizing B12 deficiency can allow neurologic injury to progress; interpret the complete clinical and laboratory picture.

Part 6 — Acute blood loss and GI bleeding

Acute hemorrhage may initially be normocytic and the hemoglobin may not immediately reflect total blood loss before equilibration. The key priorities are hemodynamics and ongoing bleeding: tachycardia, hypotension, syncope, chest pain, dyspnea, melena, hematemesis, hematochezia, severe abdominal pain, or altered mentation require urgent/emergency assessment. Do not use a single “acceptable” hemoglobin result to dismiss a patient with unstable physiology or ongoing bleeding.

Part 7 — Hemolysis

Hemolysis means premature red-cell destruction. The marrow may respond with reticulocytosis; bilirubin and LDH can rise, haptoglobin can fall, and jaundice/dark urine may occur depending on the mechanism. Causes include immune disease, medications, mechanical destruction, infections, inherited disorders, and microangiopathic processes. Hemolysis with severe symptoms, rapidly falling hemoglobin, neurologic changes, kidney injury, thrombocytopenia, or pregnancy-related complications is not a routine outpatient problem.

Part 8 — Primary versus secondary hemostasis

Primary hemostasis involves platelets and von Willebrand factor forming an initial platelet plug. Problems often cause mucocutaneous bleeding: petechiae, bruising, epistaxis, gum bleeding, or heavy menstrual bleeding. Secondary hemostasis uses clotting factors to generate fibrin and stabilize the plug. Factor-related problems more often cause deep-tissue bleeding, hemarthrosis, large hematomas, or delayed bleeding after procedures.

Medication review is central: antiplatelet drugs, anticoagulants, NSAIDs, supplements, and alcohol exposure may change bleeding risk. A normal basic screening test does not override concerning active bleeding or unstable vital signs.

Part 9 — Thrombosis: Virchow’s triad

Thrombosis becomes more likely when one or more elements of Virchow’s triad are present: venous stasis, endothelial injury, and hypercoagulability. Immobility, surgery, trauma, cancer, pregnancy/postpartum state, estrogen exposure, obesity, older age, prior VTE, thrombophilia, and family history can raise risk.

DVT commonly causes unilateral swelling, pain/tenderness, warmth, or erythema, but many DVTs are asymptomatic. Cellulitis, muscle injury, superficial thrombophlebitis, and venous insufficiency can mimic it. Use clinical probability and appropriate imaging; do not diagnose or exclude DVT from appearance alone.

Part 10 — PE: a hematology emergency with pulmonary consequences

A PE occurs when thrombus, often from the deep veins, travels to the pulmonary circulation. It can cause sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis, lightheadedness, syncope, hypoxemia, hypotension, and right-heart strain. PE can occur without visible leg symptoms. It demands the same probability-based thinking introduced in Lesson 15.

Suspected PE with instability, syncope, hypotension, marked hypoxemia, severe dyspnea, or concerning chest pain requires immediate emergency evaluation. In stable patients, testing should follow clinical probability; neither D-dimer nor a single symptom should be used in isolation.

Case 1 — Microcytic anemia with a hidden cause

A 63-year-old man has fatigue, exertional dyspnea, microcytosis, and iron deficiency. The correct reasoning is not simply “start iron.” Iron deficiency is a finding; in this context, occult GI blood loss is a clinically important possibility that needs appropriate evaluation.

Case 2 — Bleeding with instability

A patient taking an anticoagulant reports black stools, dizziness, tachycardia, and near-syncope. The first issue is possible significant GI bleeding with reduced perfusion—not the exact long-term anemia subtype. Arrange emergency assessment.

Case 3 — Unilateral leg swelling

A patient has new unilateral calf swelling and tenderness after surgery. Apply Virchow’s triad: endothelial injury + reduced mobility + postoperative hypercoagulability raise DVT probability. Prompt clinical evaluation and appropriate imaging are needed; if dyspnea or chest pain develops, consider PE emergency escalation.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. For anemia: assess stability, rate of change, symptoms, MCV, reticulocytes, and mechanism—loss, low production, or destruction.
  2. For bleeding: identify active bleeding, medication risks, platelet-versus-factor pattern, and hemodynamic compromise.
  3. For thrombosis: apply Virchow’s triad and clinical probability; use targeted testing.
  4. Always connect hematology to cardiopulmonary reserve: anemia and bleeding can provoke ischemia or shock; VTE can cause PE.
  5. Escalate immediately for instability, active major bleeding, syncope, chest pain, severe dyspnea/hypoxemia, or suspected PE.

High-Yield Summary

Anemia: low hemoglobin reduces oxygen content; classify by MCV and marrow response.
Reticulocytes: high response suggests loss/destruction; low response suggests production problem.
Iron deficiency: identify the cause, including occult blood loss when appropriate.
Primary hemostasis: platelets/vWF → mucocutaneous bleeding.
Secondary hemostasis: clotting factors/fibrin → deep-tissue bleeding.
Virchow’s triad: stasis + endothelial injury + hypercoagulability.
Red flags: hemodynamic compromise, active major bleeding, symptomatic severe anemia, suspected DVT with PE symptoms, or suspected unstable PE require emergency care.
